_note: A small, versioned, curated set of techniques per age band. Reviewed by ordinary code review, not retrieval. A clinician should review the content fields before launch.

13-15.frame: Early teens are building identity and testing limits. Lead with warmth, keep boundaries clear and few, and explain the reasoning behind a rule rather than just stating it.

techniqueNotes.validation: Name the feeling before the facts. Early teens often can't yet separate the two.
techniqueNotes.open_question: Ask about the specific moment, not the whole pattern, to avoid sounding like an interrogation.
techniqueNotes.autonomy_offer: Offer a bounded choice (two or three options), not an open-ended one, since the scaffolding still needs structure.
techniqueNotes.repair: Keep the apology short and concrete. Over-explaining can read as asking the teen to reassure the parent.
techniqueNotes.boundary: State the limit once, calmly, and let it stand. Repeating it under stress can read as nagging.

16-17.frame: Older teens want more say in decisions that affect them and are rehearsing independence. Autonomy support and genuine curiosity land better than directives.

techniqueNotes.validation: Validate the underlying want (independence, belonging) even while holding a limit.
techniqueNotes.open_question: Ask what they think a fair outcome looks like before proposing one.
techniqueNotes.autonomy_offer: Offer real input into the 'how', even where the 'whether' isn't negotiable.
techniqueNotes.repair: Acknowledge the specific thing that went wrong, and ask what would help going forward.
techniqueNotes.boundary: Frame the boundary in terms of safety or a shared value, not just 'because I said so'.

18-22.frame: This age band is transitional: some live independently, some don't. Default to adult-to-adult framing while leaving room for continued support.

techniqueNotes.validation: Validate as you would with a peer navigating a hard stretch, not as a parent soothing a child.
techniqueNotes.open_question: Ask open questions about their plan or thinking rather than offering unsolicited advice first.
techniqueNotes.autonomy_offer: Make clear the decision is theirs; offer help only if and how they want it.
techniqueNotes.repair: Name your part plainly. Avoid over-explaining your intentions.
techniqueNotes.boundary: Frame limits as your own needs or resources ('what I can offer'), not as rules over them.

23+.frame: Fully adult children. No claim to parental authority. Conversations work best framed as one adult to another, with the parent naming their own worry before any ask.

techniqueNotes.validation: Validate their autonomy explicitly; they don't need permission to make their own choices.
techniqueNotes.open_question: Ask rather than assume; your adult child's life has context you may not have.
techniqueNotes.autonomy_offer: Offer support as an option they can decline without consequence.
techniqueNotes.repair: Keep it adult-to-adult: a direct acknowledgment, not an over-apology that asks for reassurance.
techniqueNotes.boundary: Frame limits as your own boundary ('here's what I can do'), never as a rule you're imposing on them.

parent.frame: Speaking as the child's parent, with ordinary parental authority and history.

step_parent.frame: Speaking as a step-parent; authority may be newer or shared with a biological parent. Avoid assuming default authority, and lean on relationship-building language.

grandparent.frame: Speaking as a grandparent raising or co-raising a grandchild; likely has long relational history and may hold caregiving authority, but watch for era-specific assumptions about how teens/young adults communicate.

aunt_uncle.frame: Speaking as an aunt or uncle, often a supporting rather than primary authority figure. Frame suggestions as support and trust-building rather than rule enforcement, unless the parent profile indicates otherwise.

foster_parent.frame: Speaking as a foster parent; relationship history may be short and trust-building is central. Avoid presuming shared history or assuming permanence.

legal_guardian.frame: Speaking as a legal guardian with caregiving authority but not necessarily a long biological or historical relationship. Be warm without assuming shared history.

other.frame: Speaking as this child's primary caregiver in a non-standard family role. Stay warm and avoid assuming a specific relationship history.

goalNotes.repair: Lead with naming what happened and the parent's part in it before any ask.
goalNotes.closeness: Favor validation and open questions; this isn't the moment for a boundary-setting starter.
goalNotes.set_a_limit: At least one starter should be tagged 'boundary', framed per the age band's guidance above.
goalNotes.make_an_ask: Favor open_question and autonomy_offer; frame the ask so the other person can say no.
goalNotes.check_in: Keep it light and low-stakes. Favor validation and open_question; this is not the moment for a boundary starter.
goalNotes.share_feelings: The parent is the one sharing here. Starters should model naming a feeling plainly, without blaming language, and invite the other person to respond rather than just receive it.
goalNotes.give_feedback: Favor validation before the feedback itself, and open_question to check how it landed. Avoid anything that reads as a verdict on the person rather than a specific action.
goalNotes.celebrate: Keep it short and specific to what's being celebrated. Favor validation; a boundary or autonomy_offer starter rarely belongs here.

selfCriticalParentGuidance: When the parent's confidence/load score is low, no starter or 'why' line may imply the parent caused the problem or should feel guilty. Lead the 'before_you_start' line with reassurance, not a caveat.

anticipatedReactionsGuidance._source: Not copied from any published instrument. The three reaction archetypes used as a reference point (shutdown/stonewalling, deflection, pushback) are loosely inspired by Gottman's 'Four Horsemen' communication-breakdown research (criticism, contempt, defensiveness, stonewalling) and by Gottman-style emotion-coaching guidance on responding to a child who withdraws rather than engages. This is an original, best-effort adaptation for rehearsal purposes, not a validated clinical framework.
anticipatedReactionsGuidance.note: Cover a range across the 2-3 reactions returned (e.g. one shutdown/silence, one deflection, one verbal pushback) rather than three variations of the same reaction type, so the parent rehearses more than one kind of moment.
